Lunar Sparks – Small Sparks, Giant Discoveries

Lunar Sparks is a team of aspiring innovators passionate about space exploration, science, and engineering. Participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to combine creativity, technical knowledge, and problem-solving to develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges. We believe that small ideas can lead to giant discoveries, and we strive to turn our curiosity into meaningful technological solutions for Earth and beyond.
summary:
ASTRA NOVA is an interactive 3D web-based educational game designed to provide an immersive experience of astronaut training, space exploration and planetary research. Players begin their journey on Earth by learning about space science, astronaut skills, rocket systems, electrical and electronic components, and spacecraft operations. They can design and customise rockets and planetary rovers according to the environmental conditions of their selected destination.

After completing mission preparation and safety assessments, players launch their spacecraft, travel through space and explore different planets and moons. Astronauts can remotely operate rovers to investigate planetary surfaces, collect soil, rock, mineral and ice samples, and analyse scientific data using onboard laboratory systems. The simulator also includes power management, environmental hazards, communication systems and astronaut safety assessments.

The main objective is to combine space science, engineering, robotics and scientific discovery in an engaging educational experience while helping players understand the challenges of future human planetary exploration and habitability research.
details:
Project Overview

Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational simulation platform that immerses users in the full cycle of planetary exploration—from Earth-based astronaut training and spacecraft engineering through launch, interplanetary travel, remote rover operations, scientific analysis, and decision-making about human surface activity. Users progress through structured mission phases while learning real space-science principles, engineering constraints, and planetary environmental challenges.

How It Works

Users begin with astronaut training modules covering space science fundamentals, spacecraft systems (electrical, electronic, power management, and life support), and the specific hazards of chosen Solar System destinations (extreme temperatures, atmospheric pressure or vacuum, radiation, dust, terrain, and other environmental factors).

They then design and configure a rocket and specialized rover matched to the selected planet or moon, explicitly identifying risks and applying engineering mitigations (thermal protection, power architecture using solar panels and rechargeable batteries where appropriate, radiation shielding, dust mitigation, terrain mobility, and redundancy against equipment failure).

After a simulated launch and transit, the spacecraft lands and deploys the rover. The astronaut remains inside the lander and remotely operates or supervises the rover via onboard computers and communication systems. The rover, equipped with cameras, sensors, and scientific instruments, explores the surface, analyzes rocks and soil, searches for water/ice, identifies minerals and chemical compounds (both familiar terrestrial ones and potentially novel compositions), and collects samples for transfer back to the spacecraft.

The astronaut then processes the returned samples and telemetry using virtual laboratory tools to assess composition, resources, environmental conditions, and potential habitability. Before any EVA, the system evaluates whether current spacesuit technology and local conditions allow an acceptable safety margin; otherwise exploration continues remotely. Failure modes, resource limits, and cascading system interactions are simulated so users experience realistic trade-offs.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The platform makes complex, multi-disciplinary space-exploration challenges accessible and engaging for students and the general public. It builds practical understanding of systems engineering, risk assessment, power and life-support design, robotic exploration, and planetary science while fostering scientific curiosity and problem-solving skills. By linking training, engineering decisions, remote operations, and scientific discovery in one continuous experience, it helps prepare the next generation of explorers and informed citizens who can appreciate the real difficulties and opportunities of expanding human presence beyond Earth.

Tools, Technologies, and Development Approach

The simulation is built as a modular, browser-based interactive application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the core interface, visuals, and interactivity. Planetary environment data, mission parameters, rover configurations, and scientific results are structured and loaded using JSON. The architecture is designed to be lightweight and accessible through a standard web browser, allowing users to experience astronaut training, spacecraft design, launch, remote rover operations, and sample analysis without requiring heavy software installations. Educational content is organized around validated NASA and planetary-science references. The modular structure makes it easy to add new destinations, instruments, or mission scenarios in the future.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Creativity lies in treating the entire mission arc—training, design under constraint, launch, remote science operations, sample analysis, and EVA go/no-go decisions—as a single coherent, consequence-driven experience rather than isolated lessons or games. Users must actively confront real planetary differences and engineering trade-offs instead of following a linear tutorial.

The team considered scientific accuracy versus playability, progressive difficulty suitable for secondary-school through university learners, accessibility across devices, clear visualization of invisible hazards (radiation, power margins, thermal extremes), and the educational value of failure and recovery. Emphasis was placed on systems thinking: power, thermal, mobility, communications, and science instruments interact, so an early design choice can cascade into later mission outcomes. Safety evaluation before EVA and the preference for remote operations when conditions are hostile reinforce realistic operational philosophy.
